author: Declaration Desk
title: Supreme Court sends Trinamool's plea against 10 rebel MLAs to Calcutta High Court
dek: The court asked the High Court to hear urgently the faction's demand that the Speaker decide disqualification petitions pending since July, but refused to step in itself.
body:
The Supreme Court on Thursday declined to hear the Trinamool Congress's plea to make the West Bengal Assembly Speaker decide whether 10 rebel party MLAs should be disqualified, and sent it to the Calcutta High Court, asking that court to hear it urgently.

A bench of Chief Justice Surya Kant and Justice Joymalya Bagchi disposed of the petition filed by Sovandeb Chattopadhyay, a senior MLA of the Mamata Banerjee-led Trinamool, and gave him liberty to file a fresh petition in the High Court. It asked the High Court's Chief Justice to list the case before a division bench for urgent consideration and an early decision, according to reports. "It seems to us that the petitioner has to take recourse to the Calcutta High Court," the bench said.

## The dispute

Trinamool filed petitions on 8 July seeking the disqualification of 10 MLAs who were elected on its ticket and then broke with the party after it lost this year's Assembly election to the BJP. They are Ritabrata Banerjee, Firhad Hakim, Arup Roy, Sandipan Saha, Akhruzzaman Ansari, Shiuli Saha, Sabina Yasmin, Biplab Mitra, Javed Khan and Rathin Ghosh, reports said.

The anti-defection law in the Tenth Schedule of the Constitution leaves the decision to the Speaker. The Speaker, Rathindra Bose, has not ruled on the petitions. Instead he recognised Ritabrata Banerjee, one of the rebels, as Leader of the Opposition, and another rebel as chief whip, although the Mamata Banerjee faction had named Mr Chattopadhyay for the post. On 18 June, the Calcutta High Court refused to pass an interim order against the Speaker's decision on the Leader of the Opposition, and reports said that the High Court later delivered a split verdict on that dispute.

This was Mr Chattopadhyay's second attempt in the Supreme Court. In September he had sought a direction to the Speaker; the court then said it had no reason to doubt the Speaker and hoped he would decide within the timelines set in an earlier Manipur case, Keisham Meghachandra Singh, in which the court said such petitions should normally be decided within three months, reports said.

## In court

Mr Chattopadhyay's counsel told the bench that the July petitions had still not been decided, reports said. He asked the court to send the case directly to a division bench of the High Court so it would not be caught up in appeals within that court, and noted that the High Court is on its annual break until mid-November.

The bench agreed to the request for a division bench but refused to hear the case itself. "You cannot litigate to jump the queue," Justice Bagchi said, according to reports. He added that the court could not have all such petitions come to it "merely because we have passed an order in one". Counsel had pointed out that the court had already passed an order in another case concerning West Bengal.

The Speaker's office and the rebel MLAs had not publicly responded to the order by Thursday afternoon.

## Why it matters

The fight is over who speaks for the opposition in the Assembly after the BJP's win. If the 10 MLAs were disqualified, they would lose their seats and by-elections would follow. While the petitions remain undecided, the rebels keep their seats and the posts of Leader of the Opposition and chief whip.

## What happens next

Mr Chattopadhyay is expected to file a petition in the Calcutta High Court, where regular benches resume after the break. The Supreme Court's request means it should go straight to a division bench of two judges. The dispute comes as parties prepare for elections to the Kolkata, Howrah and Siliguri municipal corporations, for which the High Court has barred a poll notice while it considers the new Kolkata ward map.
